title: The New Measure of Influence: What Matters in Prestige Beauty Now
description: Follower count no longer defines influence. Discover the metrics, expertise and creator mix that matter most for prestige beauty brands in 2026.

For years, follower count dominated influencer marketing. It determined who made the consideration list, who commanded the highest fees, and often, who brands believed had the greatest influence. As a standalone measure of influence, follower count is increasingly a vanity metric.

Here’s why: Social feeds are no longer distributed primarily to a creator’s followers. Today, algorithms increasingly distribute content based on interest and engagement rather than followers alone, meaning a creator’s reach can extend far beyond - or short of - their follower count. In fact, nearly half (49%) of Instagram views now come from non-followers, and 58% of views on TikTok come from the For You page, according to Dash Social’s 2026 Social Media Benchmark Report.

Beyond views, consumers are also placing less importance on influencer follower counts. According to Sprout Social’s 2026 Influencer Marketing Report, only 17% of consumers check a creator's follower count before deciding whether to engage, with audiences placing greater importance on subject relevance and content style. If consumers themselves aren't using follower count as a primary signal of influence, marketers shouldn't either.

For prestige beauty, the implications are significant. Beauty purchases are personal. Consumers want to know how a foundation sits on real skin, whether a serum is worth the investment, how a lipstick looks in natural light or whether a hair product actually works on their texture. Authority comes from specificity, experience and trust - not follower counts.

As influencer marketing has matured, so has our ability to measure what actually makes a creator valuable. Follower count is now just one signal among many. Affiliate conversion rate. Click-throughs. Saves and shares. Audience demographics. Content quality. Category expertise. Together, these signals tell us far more about a creator’s ability to drive consideration and action than audience size alone.

As Forbes notes, “scale alone does not guarantee impact.” An important point for marketers: the brief shouldn't begin with a minimum follower count, but with the audience behavior the brand needs to drive. A creator driving awareness should not necessarily be measured the same way as one tasked with educating consumers, generating consideration or converting sales.
Prestige beauty raises the stakes even further.

As price points rise, so does the burden of persuasion. Consumers need a reason to believe a $90 serum, $60 foundation or luxury hair treatment deserves a place in their routine. That's where creator credibility becomes critical. A dermatologist explaining clinical results. A makeup artist demonstrating formulation and technique. A hair stylist speaking specifically to texture. That kind of influence is built through accumulated trust.

For prestige beauty brands, incorporating professional voices such as dermatologists, estheticians, makeup artists and hairstylists can add a critical layer of authority to a creator program. Their value comes from the expertise behind the recommendation: they can educate consumers on ingredients, formulation and technique, validate product performance, and help articulate what meaningfully differentiates a product from its competitors. For these creators, professional authority and category expertise matters far more than audience size.

The strongest creator programs are built around the role each creator plays in achieving the brand’s objectives. The opportunity is in the mix. Rather than defaulting to audience size, marketers should consider what they need each creator to accomplish and select talent accordingly. If the goal is awareness, scale may matter. If the goal is credibility, expertise may matter more. If the goal is conversion, historical performance may tell you considerably more than audience size ever could.

Further, reach isn’t confined to the audience a creator has already built. As Business of Fashion notes, much of the audience being served creator content may not follow that creator. In an algorithm-driven feed, the right content can travel well beyond the creator’s existing community making relevance, creative quality and audience response increasingly important parts of the equation.
As influencer marketing becomes more measurable, the way brands define influence needs to evolve with it.
Follower count tells you who clicked “follow.” Influence tells you who’s still listening.
